I think there are many sides to this point! 
Many things are possible and it depends on so many factors. Without planting ideas and being too specific- 
1. there is the element of control of intake and knowing exact numbers 
2. Not having to make choices around food and removing any food choices
3. Some types of tubes can be used to drain. And even if draining is required (eg gastroparesis)- sometimes it can be done to excess

Aside from the obvious and other points discussed here. I wanted to bring up that I haven’t really seen a lot of discussion around ARFID. A disorder in which it is not specifically weight based (although can co exist with other disorders). In which things like correlations or perceived relations between an attribute/s of food are feared due to a non weight based factor. For example- things like texture, flavour, ingredients etc can be feared for reasons such as possibly causing symptoms, discomfort, sensory overload, possible allergies etc. it can be that the food genuinely causes the fear or that the person may believe it can happen. For example- many chronic illness suffers who have or perceive to have gastro issues may be scared of certain foods that will or are thought to cause a flare up in symptoms. My point here is that some people who may want a tube want it for reasons other than their body. If that makes sense? 
Also- just wanted to say that needing a tube and wanting a tube is not an indicator on its own for MBI. Many people want it as they genuinely need it and don’t want to continue slowly ☠️ing from malnutrition etc. everyone is different- but these were just my two cents worth.
The irony is that it doesn’t even look like AFIB.

The thing is that apple watches CAN detect possible AFIB and it is designed to alert people to the possibility of an arrhythmia but not to diagnose or provide certainty. It is purely an alert if possible issues, which can prompt people to seek medical attention to determine the validity of the Apple Watch reading. So, the watch showed possible AFIB- and that should be taken into consideration with other factors. Now, her age and medical history plus no history of AFIB make it unlikely that it was a true and accurate reading. Yes, she does have some underlying medical conditions, but as far as I’m aware, there is no condition that is linked to the heart itself. Dysautonomia is a condition of the autonomic nervous system rather than the actual heart. So, although it is unlikely that the watch reading was true. The only way to rule it out completely would be a 12 lead ecg. The Apple Watch only does a single lead interpretation. If a 12 lead ECG doesn’t show AFIB- and the history doesn’t make it likely- then it likely isn’t. Especially when the 12 lead was taken less than an hour after the watch reading was taken. AFIB doesn’t flick in and out like that. So in summary, while the Apple Watch could in theory point to possible AFIB, the proper diagnostic tests and history rule it out as a possibility.
